danish.title: Tiende bog (1812) — Kapitel 10
paragraphs: Efter sin fars begravelse lukkede fyrstinde Marja sig inde på sit værelse og lod ingen komme ind. En pige kom til døren for at sige, at Alpatytj bad om ordrer vedrørende deres afrejse. (Det var før hans samtale med Dron.) Fyrstinde Marja rejste sig på sofaen, hvor hun havde ligget, og svarede gennem den lukkede dør, at hun ikke agtede at rejse og bad om at blive ladt i fred.

Vinduerne i det værelse, hvor hun lå, vendte mod vest. Hun lå på sofaen med ansigtet mod væggen og fingerede ved knapperne på læderpuden, uden at se andet end den pude, og hendes forvirrede tanker kredsede om ét emne — dødens uigenkaldelighed og hendes egen åndelige lavhed, som hun ikke havde anet, men som var kommet frem under hendes fars sygdom. Hun ønskede at bede, men turde ikke, turde ikke i sin nuværende sindstilstand henvende sig til Gud. Hun lå længe i den stilling.

Solen var nået over til den anden side af huset, og dens skrå stråler skinnede ind gennem det åbne vindue og oplyste værelset og en del af safianspuden, som fyrstinde Marja kiggede på. Strømmen af hendes tanker standsede pludselig. Ubevidst satte hun sig op, glattede sit hår, rejste sig og gik hen til vinduet, idet hun ufrivilligt indåndede den friske, klare men blæsende aftens luft.
»Ja, nu kan du nyde aftenen! Han er borte, og ingen vil hindre dig,« sagde hun til sig selv og sank ned i en stol, lod hovedet falde mod vindueskarmen.

Nogen sagde hendes navn med blød og øm stemme fra haven og kyssede hendes hoved. Hun så op. Det var mademoiselle Bourienne i sort kjole og sørgeflor. Hun nærmede sig fyrstinde Marja blødt, sukkede, kyssede hende og begyndte straks at græde. Fyrstinden så op på hende. Al deres tidligere disharmoni og hendes egen jalousi vendte tilbage i hendes erindring. Men hun huskede også, hvordan han i den seneste tid var forandret over for mademoiselle Bourienne og ikke kunne udholde at se hende, hvorved han viste, hvor uretfærdige de bebrejdelser var, fyrstinde Marja i tankerne havde rettet mod hende. »Desuden, er det min sag — jeg, der ønskede hans død — at fordømme nogen?« tænkte hun.

Fyrstinde Marja forestillede sig levende mademoiselle Bouriennes stilling — hun, som hun på det seneste havde holdt på afstand, men som dog var afhængig af hende og boede i hendes hus. Hun fik ondt af hende og rakte hånden frem med et blik af blid forespørgsel. Mademoiselle Bourienne begyndte straks at græde igen og kyssede den hånd, idet hun talte om fyrstindens sorg og gjorde sig selv til delagtig i den. Hun sagde, at hendes eneste trøst var, at fyrstinden tillod hende at dele sin sorg, at alle gamle misforståelser burde synke i intet over for denne store sorg; at hun følte sig uden skyld over for alle, og at han, fra oven, så hendes hengivenhed og taknemmelighed. Fyrstinden hørte hende uden at fatte ordene, men kiggede af og til op på hende og lyttede til lyden af hendes stemme.

»Deres stilling er dobbelt frygtelig, kære fyrstinde,« sagde mademoiselle Bourienne efter en pause. »Jeg forstår, at De ikke kunne og ikke kan tænke på Dem selv, men med min kærlighed til Dem må jeg gøre det ... Har Alpatytj været hos Dem? Har han talt til Dem om at rejse?« spurgte hun.

Fyrstinde Marja svarede ikke. Hun forstod ikke, hvem der skulle rejse, eller hvorhen. »Er det muligt at planlægge eller tænke på noget nu? Er det ikke alt sammen ligegyldigt?« tænkte hun og svarede ikke.

»Ved De, chère Marie,« sagde mademoiselle Bourienne, »at vi er i fare — vi er omringet af franskmændene. Det ville være farligt at flytte sig nu. Rejser vi, er vi næsten sikre på at blive taget til fange, og Gud véd ...«
Fyrstinde Marja så på sin ledsagerske uden at forstå, hvad hun talte om.

»Å, hvis nogen vidste, hvor lidt noget som helst betyder for mig nu,« sagde hun. »Naturligvis ville jeg på ingen måde ønske at forlade ham ... Alpatytj sagde godt nok noget om at rejse ... Tal med ham; jeg kan intet, intet, og vil ikke ...«

»Jeg har talt med ham. Han håber, vi kan nå at komme af sted i morgen, men jeg synes, det nu ville være bedre at blive her,« sagde mademoiselle Bourienne. »For De vil give mig ret, chère Marie — at falde i hænderne på soldater eller oprørske bønder ville være frygteligt.«

Mademoiselle Bourienne tog fra sin ridikule en proklamation (ikke trykt på almindeligt russisk papir) fra general Rameau, der sagde folk, de ikke skulle forlade deres hjem, og at de franske myndigheder ville yde dem ordentlig beskyttelse. Hun rakte den til fyrstinden.
»Jeg synes, det bedste ville være at henvende sig til den general,« fortsatte hun, »og jeg er sikker på, at al skyldig respekt ville blive vist Dem.«
Fyrstinde Marja læste papiret, og hendes ansigt begyndte at skælve af tilbageholdte hulken.
»Fra hvem har du fået det?« spurgte hun.
»De har formentlig genkendt, at jeg er fransk, på mit navn,« svarede mademoiselle Bourienne rødmende.
Fyrstinde Marja rejste sig med papiret i hånden fra vinduet, og med blegt ansigt gik hun ud af værelset og ind i det, der havde været fyrst Andrejs arbejdsværelse.

»Dunjasja, send Alpatytj eller Drónusjka eller nogen til mig!« sagde hun, »og sig til mademoiselle Bourienne, at hun ikke skal komme ind til mig,« tilføjede hun, da hun hørte mademoiselle Bouriennes stemme. »Vi må af sted med det samme, med det samme!« sagde hun, forfærdet ved tanken om at blive efterladt i franskmændenes hænder.

»Hvis fyrst Andrej hørte, at jeg var i franskmændenes magt! At jeg, fyrst Nikolaj Bolkonskijs datter, bad general Rameau om beskyttelse og modtog hans gunst!« Denne tanke forfærdede hende, fik hende til at gyse, rødme og føle en bølge af vrede og stolthed, som hun aldrig havde oplevet før. Alt det ydmygende og især alt det nedværdigende i hendes situation stod hende levende klart for øje. »De, franskmændene, ville slå sig ned i dette hus: monsieur le général Rameau ville indtage fyrst Andrejs arbejdsværelse og more sig med at gennemse og læse hans breve og papirer. Mademoiselle Bourienne ville gøre Bogutjarovos honnører for ham. Jeg ville blive tildelt et lille værelse som en gunstbevisning — soldaterne ville krænke min fars nygravede grav for at stjæle hans kors og stjerner, de ville fortælle mig om deres sejre over russerne og lade, som om de havde medfølelse med min sorg ...« tænkte fyrstinde Marja, ikke med egne tanker, men med en følelse af at være bundet til at tænke som sin far og bror. For sin egen skyld var hun ligeglad med, hvor hun blev, eller hvad der skete med hende, men hun følte sig som repræsentant for sin afdøde far og for fyrst Andrej. Ufrivilligt tænkte hun deres tanker og følte deres følelser. Hvad de ville have sagt og gjort, følte hun sig forpligtet til at sige og gøre. Hun gik ind i fyrst Andrejs arbejdsværelse, forsøgte helt at sætte sig ind i hans tanker og overvejede sin situation.
De krav, livet stillede, som var forekommet hende tilintetgjort af hendes fars død, rejste sig pludselig for hende med en ny, hidtil ukendt kraft og tog magten over hende.

Ophidset og rødmende gik hun frem og tilbage i værelset og sendte snart bud efter Mikhail Ivanovitj, snart efter Tikhon eller Dron. Dunjasja, ammen og de andre piger kunne ikke sige, i hvor høj grad mademoiselle Bouriennes udsagn var korrekt. Alpatytj var ikke hjemme — han var taget til politimyndigheden. Heller ikke arkitekten Mikhail Ivanovitj, der blev sendt bud efter og kom med søvnige øjne, kunne fortælle fyrstinde Marja noget. Med det samme bifaldende smil, som han i femten år havde været vant til at besvare den gamle fyrste med, uden at udtrykke egne synspunkter, svarede han nu fyrstinde Marja, så intet bestemt kunne uddrages af hans svar. Den gamle kammertjener Tikhon, med sit indfaldne, udmarvede ansigt præget af utrøstelig sorg, svarede: »Ja, fyrstinde« til alle fyrstinde Marjas spørgsmål og kunne næppe holde gråden tilbage, når han så på hende.
Endelig trådte Dron, landsbyældsten, ind i stuen og bukkede dybt for fyrstinde Marja, hvorefter han stillede sig ved dørkarmen.
Fyrstinde Marja gik op og ned i stuen og standsede foran ham.

»Drónusjka,« sagde hun og betragtede ham som en sikker ven — denne Drónusjka, der altid plejede at bringe en særlig slags honningkager med fra sit besøg på markedet i Vjazma hvert år og smilende byde hende dem — »Drónusjka, nu efter vores ulykke ...« begyndte hun, men kunne ikke fortsætte.
»Vi er alle i Guds hånd,« sagde han med et suk.
De var tavse et stykke tid.
»Drónusjka, Alpatytj er rejst et sted hen, og jeg har ingen at henvende mig til. Er det sandt, som de siger mig, at jeg ikke engang kan rejse bort?«
»Hvorfor skulle De ikke kunne rejse, Deres excellence? Det kan De sagtens,« sagde Dron.
»Man har sagt mig, at det er farligt på grund af fjenden. Kære ven, jeg kan intet. Jeg forstår intet. Jeg har ingen! Jeg vil rejse i aften eller tidligt i morgen.«
Dron tøvede. Han kiggede skævt på fyrstinde Marja og sagde: »Der er ingen heste; det sagde jeg Jakov Alpatytj.«
»Hvorfor er der ingen?« spurgte fyrstinden.

»Det er Guds straf over os,« sagde Dron. »De heste, vi havde, er taget til hæren, eller de er døde — det er et sådant år! Det handler ikke om at fodre heste — vi kan selv dø af sult! Somme tider går folk tre dage uden at spise. Vi har intet, vi er ruinerede.«
Fyrstinde Marja lyttede opmærksomt til, hvad han fortalte hende.
»Bønderne er ruinerede? De har intet brød?« spurgte hun.
»De dør af sult,« sagde Dron. »Det handler ikke om vogne.«
»Men hvorfor har du ikke sagt det til mig, Drónusjka? Er det ikke muligt at hjælpe dem? Jeg vil gøre alt, hvad jeg kan ...«

For fyrstinde Marja var det mærkeligt, at der nu — i et øjeblik, da en sådan sorg fyldte hendes sjæl — kunne være rige og fattige, og at de rige kunne undlade at hjælpe de fattige. Hun havde vagt hørt, at der fandtes noget, der hed »herregårdskorn«, som undertiden blev givet til bønderne. Hun vidste også, at hverken hendes far eller bror ville nægte at hjælpe bønder i nød; hun frygtede blot at begå en fejl i sin tale om uddelingen af det korn, hun ønskede at give. Hun var glad for, at sådanne bekymringer bød sig, da de gjorde det muligt for hende uden skrupler at glemme sin egen sorg. Hun begyndte at spørge Dron om bøndernes behov, og hvad der i Bogutjarovo tilhørte godsejeren.
»Men vi har vel korn, der tilhører min bror?« sagde hun.
»Godsejerens korn er alt sammen i behold,« svarede Dron stolt. »Vores fyrste gav ikke ordre til at sælge det.«
»Giv det til bønderne, lad dem få alt, hvad de har brug for; jeg giver dig tilladelse i min brors navn,« sagde hun.
Dron svarede ikke, men sukkede dybt.
»Giv dem det korn, hvis der er nok. Del det hele ud. Jeg giver denne ordre i min brors navn; og sig dem, at hvad der er vores, er deres. Vi unde dem alt. Sig dem det.«
Dron betragtede fyrstinden opmærksomt, mens hun talte.
»Fritag mig, lille moder, for Guds skyld! Befal at nøglerne bliver taget fra mig,« sagde han. »Jeg har tjent i tre og tyve år og har ingen uret gjort. Fritag mig, for Guds skyld!«

Fyrstinde Marja forstod ikke, hvad han ønskede af hende, eller hvorfor han bad om at blive fritaget. Hun svarede, at hun aldrig havde tvivlet på hans hengivenhed, og at hun var rede til at gøre alt for ham og for bønderne.

english.title: Book Ten (1812) — Chapter 10
paragraphs: After her father's funeral, Princess Mary shut herself up in her room and refused to see anyone. A maid came to the door to say that Alpatych was asking for orders about their departure. (This was before his talk with Dron.) Princess Mary raised herself from the sofa where she had been lying and replied through the closed door that she didn't intend to go anywhere and asked to be left in peace.

The windows of the room where she lay faced west. She lay on the sofa with her face to the wall, fingering the buttons of the leather cushion and seeing nothing but that cushion, and her confused thoughts centered on one subject—the finality of death and her own spiritual baseness, which she had not suspected but which had revealed itself during her father's illness. She wanted to pray but didn't dare—couldn't, in her present state of mind, address herself to God. She lay there for a long time.

The sun had moved to the other side of the house, and its slanting rays shone through the open window, lighting up the room and part of the leather cushion Princess Mary was looking at. The flow of her thoughts suddenly stopped. Unconsciously she sat up, smoothed her hair, got up, and went to the window, involuntarily breathing in the freshness of the clear but windy evening.
"Yes, you can enjoy the evening now! He's gone and no one will stand in your way," she said to herself, and sinking into a chair, she let her head fall on the windowsill.

Someone spoke her name in a soft and tender voice from the garden and kissed her head. She looked up. It was Mademoiselle Bourienne in a black dress and mourning cap. She softly approached Princess Mary, sighed, kissed her, and immediately began to cry. The princess looked at her. All their former friction and her own jealousy came back to her mind. But she also remembered how he had changed lately toward Mademoiselle Bourienne and could no longer bear the sight of her—showing how unjust the reproaches Princess Mary had mentally leveled at her had been. "Besides, is it for me—I who wished for his death—to condemn anyone?" she thought.

Princess Mary vividly pictured to herself the position of Mademoiselle Bourienne, whom she had recently kept at a distance but who was still dependent on her and living in her house. She felt sorry for her and held out her hand with a look of gentle inquiry. Mademoiselle Bourienne immediately began crying again and kissed that hand, speaking of the princess's sorrow and claiming a share in it. She said her only consolation was that the princess allowed her to share her grief, that all the old misunderstandings should vanish before this great sorrow; that she felt herself blameless toward everyone, and that he, from above, saw her devotion and gratitude. The princess listened, not following the words but occasionally looking up at her and listening to the sound of her voice.

"Your position is doubly terrible, dear princess," said Mademoiselle Bourienne after a pause. "I understand that you could not, and cannot, think of yourself, but with my love for you I must do so... Has Alpatych been to you? Has he spoken to you of leaving?" she asked.
Princess Mary did not answer. She didn't understand who was supposed to go or where. "Is it possible to plan or think about anything now? Does anything matter?" she thought, and made no reply.

"You know, dear Marie," said Mademoiselle Bourienne, "that we are in danger—we are surrounded by the French. It would be dangerous to move now. If we try to go, we will almost certainly be taken prisoner, and God knows..."
Princess Mary looked at her companion without understanding what she was saying.

"Oh, if anyone knew how little anything matters to me now," she said. "Of course I would never want to leave him... Alpatych did say something about going... Speak to him; I can do nothing, nothing, and don't want to..."

"I've spoken to him. He hopes we can still get away tomorrow, but I think it would be better to stay here now," said Mademoiselle Bourienne. "Because, you must agree, dear Marie, to fall into the hands of soldiers or riotous peasants would be terrible."

Mademoiselle Bourienne took from her bag a proclamation (not printed on standard Russian paper) by General Rameau, telling people not to leave their homes and promising that the French authorities would provide proper protection. She handed it to the princess.
"I think it would be best to appeal to that general," she continued. "I'm sure that you would be shown all due respect."
Princess Mary read the paper, and her face began to quiver with stifled sobs.
"Who gave you this?" she asked.
"They probably recognized that I am French, by my name," replied Mademoiselle Bourienne, blushing.
Princess Mary, paper in hand, rose from the window and with a pale face walked out of the room and into what had been Prince Andrew's study.

"Dunyasha! Send Alpatych, or Dronushka, or somebody to me!" she said, "and tell Mademoiselle Bourienne not to come to me," she added, hearing Mademoiselle Bourienne's voice. "We must go at once, at once!" she said, appalled at the thought of being left to the mercy of the French.

"If Prince Andrew found out I was in the power of the French! That I, the daughter of Prince Nicholas Bolkonsky, asked General Rameau for protection and accepted his favor!" This idea horrified her, made her shudder, blush, and feel a surge of anger and pride unlike anything she had ever experienced. All that was distressing, and especially all that was humiliating, in her position rose vividly to her mind. "They, the French, would settle in this house; Monsieur le General Rameau would occupy Prince Andrew's study and amuse himself looking through his letters and papers. Mademoiselle Bourienne would play hostess for him at Bogucharovo. I would be given a small room as a favor; the soldiers would desecrate my father's freshly dug grave to steal his medals and decorations; they would tell me about their victories over the Russians and pretend to sympathize with my grief..." thought Princess Mary, not thinking her own thoughts but feeling compelled to think like her father and brother. For herself she didn't care where she stayed or what happened to her, but she felt herself the representative of her dead father and Prince Andrew. Involuntarily she thought their thoughts and felt their feelings. What they would have said and done, she felt bound to say and do. She went into Prince Andrew's study, trying to enter fully into his way of thinking, and considered her situation.
The demands of life, which had seemed annihilated by her father's death, suddenly rose before her with a new, previously unknown force and took hold of her.

Agitated and flushed, she paced the room, sending now for Michael Ivanovich and now for Tikhon or Dron. Dunyasha, the nurse, and the other maids couldn't say how accurate Mademoiselle Bourienne's claims were. Alpatych was not at home—he had gone to the police. Nor could the architect Michael Ivanovich, who came in with sleepy eyes when sent for, tell Princess Mary anything. With exactly the same smile of agreement with which he had been accustomed to respond to the old prince for fifteen years without expressing opinions of his own, he now answered Princess Mary so that nothing definite could be gathered from his replies. The old valet Tikhon, with his sunken, gaunt face bearing the stamp of inconsolable grief, replied "Yes, Princess" to all her questions and could barely hold back his sobs as he looked at her.
At length Dron, the village Elder, entered the room and with a deep bow to Princess Mary came to a halt by the doorpost.
Princess Mary walked up and down the room and stopped in front of him.

"Dronushka," she said, regarding as a trusted friend this man who always used to bring a special kind of gingerbread from his trips to the Vyazma fair every year and smilingly offer it to her, "Dronushka, now after our misfortune..." she began, but could not go on.
"We are all in God's hands," he said with a sigh.
They were silent for a while.
"Dronushka, Alpatych has gone off somewhere and I have no one to turn to. Is it true, as they tell me, that I can't even leave?"
"Why shouldn't you leave, your excellency? You can go," said Dron.
"I was told it would be dangerous because of the enemy. Dear friend, I can't manage anything. I don't understand anything. I have nobody! I want to go away tonight or early tomorrow morning."
Dron paused. He glanced sideways at Princess Mary and said: "There are no horses; I told Yakov Alpatych so."
"Why are there none?" asked the princess.

"It's all God's punishment," said Dron. "Whatever horses we had were taken for the army or died—it's been that kind of year! We can barely feed ourselves, let alone keep horses. Some go three days without eating. We've got nothing—we've been ruined."
Princess Mary listened carefully to what he told her.
"The peasants are ruined? They have no bread?" she asked.
"They're starving," said Dron. "It's not a matter of carting."
"But why didn't you tell me, Dronushka? Can't something be done to help them? I'll do everything I can..."

To Princess Mary it seemed strange that now, at a moment when such sorrow filled her soul, there could be rich and poor, and that the rich could fail to help the poor. She vaguely knew there was such a thing as "landlord's grain" that was sometimes given to the peasants. She also knew that neither her father nor her brother would refuse to help peasants in need; she only feared making some mistake in distributing the grain she wanted to give. She was glad that such practical concerns presented themselves, allowing her without guilt to forget her own grief. She began asking Dron about the peasants' needs and what belonged to the landlord at Bogucharovo.
"But we have grain belonging to my brother?" she said.
"The landlord's grain is all safe," replied Dron proudly. "Our prince gave no order to sell it."
"Give it to the peasants—let them have everything they need; I give you permission in my brother's name," she said.
Dron said nothing but sighed deeply.
"Give them that grain if there's enough. Distribute it all. I give this order in my brother's name; and tell them that what is ours is theirs. We don't grudge them anything. Tell them that."
Dron looked hard at the princess while she was speaking.
"Let me go, dear lady, for God's sake! Order the keys to be taken from me," he said. "I've served twenty-three years and done no wrong. Let me go, for God's sake!"

Princess Mary didn't understand what he wanted or why he was asking to be discharged. She replied that she had never doubted his devotion and that she was ready to do anything for him and for the peasants.
